name: Iso E Super

lead: Iso E Super is a synthetic fragrance ingredient with a smooth, woody, amber scent that stays on skin and fabric for a long time. It appears in many perfumes, in some at very high percentages, and one perfume, Molecule 01, consists of it alone.

For appearance and grooming, it matters as a way to smell clean and pleasant. Wearers describe it as a quiet skin-scent that blends with their own, and some say it makes them noticeably more attractive to others. No study has tested that claim.

paras: It is worn as a perfume, either as a single-ingredient fragrance or as part of blends, applied to skin or clothes in the usual way for perfume. People layer it under other scents.

Patch-test studies show a small share of tested patients react to it, and it is classed as a skin sensitizer. Industry guidelines set maximum use levels. Some people perceive its main scent component weakly, so they may not smell it on themselves.

chain: Soft personal scent that people find pleasant
angle.text: It is worn as perfume to add a smooth woody scent that lasts on skin and clothes. Any extra effect on attractiveness is a claim by wearers.

lead: Iso E Super is the trade name for an isomer mixture of tetramethyl acetyloctahydronaphthalenes, also known as OTNE, a synthetic woody-amber aroma-chemical.[1] It was developed at IFF in the early 1970s, patented in 1975 and first used in the perfume Halston, and became a staple of modern perfumery from the late 1980s.[1][2]

For grooming, people use it as a fragrance that sits close to the skin. Perfumer Geza Schon built the perfume Molecule 01 entirely from it and the related Escentric 01 around it at high concentration.[1][3] Some wearers say it enhances their natural scent; the claim that it attracts other people is a community belief that has not been tested in published studies.

paras: Commercial Iso E Super is a mixture of more than twenty isomeric ketones made by a Diels-Alder route.[1] Reportedly the main isomer is nearly odorless and the characteristic scent comes from a minor isomer that makes up a few percent.[1] Reviews describe it as the first synthetic ingredient used as a pure fragrance in its own right.[2]

Researchers at Dragoco, Givaudan and Firmenich worked on woody ketones from the 1950s and 1960s; IFF chemists John Hall and James Sanders created the product, and it was named Isocyclemone E before being refined as Iso E Super.[1] Fragrance reviews note that woody perfume notes still lack a replacement for it.[4]

Reported concentrations include about 25 percent in Dior Fahrenheit (1988) and 55 percent in Terre d'Hermes (2006).[1] Molecule 01 launched in 2006 as a perfume composed of it alone, and Escentric 01 uses 65 percent alongside other materials.[1][3]

Patch tests show positive reactions in roughly 0.2 to 1.7 percent of patients in three dermatology studies; it is classed as a skin sensitizer, and IFRA has published use limits since 2009. Reviews have judged it safe at current use levels.[1]

No studies found on its effects on attractiveness or skin. An olfactory study used it as one of four odorants in electrophysiological recordings from the human nose, showing no significant decline in the response across ten repeated exposures.[5]
